L10: ## NAME         cite15†top L11: 
L12:            flock - apply or remove an advisory lock on an open file
L13: 
L14: 
L15: ## LIBRARY         cite15†top L16: 
L17:            Standard C library (libc, -lc)
L18: 
L19: 
L20: ## SYNOPSIS         cite15†top L21: 
L22:            #include <sys/file.h>
L23: 
L24:            int flock(int fd, int op);
L25: ## DESCRIPTION         cite15†top L26: 
L27:            Apply or remove an advisory lock on the open file specified by fd.
L28:            The argument op is one of the following:
L29: 
L30:                LOCK_SH  Place a shared lock.  More than one process may hold
L31:                         a shared lock for a given file at a given time.
L32: 
L33:                LOCK_EX  Place an exclusive lock.  Only one process may hold
L34:                         an exclusive lock for a given file at a given time.
L35:                LOCK_UN  Remove an existing lock held by this process.
L36: 
L37:            A call to flock() may block if an incompatible lock is held by
L38:            another process.  To make a nonblocking request, include LOCK_NB
L39:            (by ORing) with any of the above operations.
L40: 
L41:            A single file may not simultaneously have both shared and
L42:            exclusive locks.
L43: 
L44:            Locks created by flock() are associated with an open file
L45:            description (see cite16†open(2) ).  This means that duplicate file
L46:            descriptors (created by, for example, cite17†fork(2) or cite18†dup(2) ) refer to
L47:            the same lock, and this lock may be modified or released using any
L48:            of these file descriptors.  Furthermore, the lock is released
L49:            either by an explicit LOCK_UN operation on any of these duplicate
L50:            file descriptors, or when all such file descriptors have been
L51:            closed.
L52:            If a process uses cite16†open(2) (or similar) to obtain more than one
L53:            file descriptor for the same file, these file descriptors are
L54:            treated independently by flock().  An attempt to lock the file
L55:            using one of these file descriptors may be denied by a lock that
L56:            the calling process has already placed via another file
L57:            descriptor.
L58: 
L59:            A process may hold only one type of lock (shared or exclusive) on
L60:            a file.  Subsequent flock() calls on an already locked file will
L61:            convert an existing lock to the new lock mode.
L62: 
L63:            Locks created by flock() are preserved across an cite19†execve(2) .
L64: 
L65:            A shared or exclusive lock can be placed on a file regardless of
L66:            the mode in which the file was opened.
L67: ## RETURN VALUE         cite15†top L68: 
L69:            On success, zero is returned.  On error, -1 is returned, and cite20†errno L70:            is set to indicate the error.
L71: ## ERRORS         cite15†top L72: 
L73:            EBADF  fd is not an open file descriptor.
L74: 
L75:            EINTR  While waiting to acquire a lock, the call was interrupted
L76:                   by delivery of a signal caught by a handler; see cite21†signal(7) .
L77: 
L78:            EINVAL op is invalid.
L79: 
L80:            ENOLCK The kernel ran out of memory for allocating lock records.
L81: 
L82:            EWOULDBLOCK
L83:                   The file is locked and the LOCK_NB flag was selected.
L84: ## VERSIONS         cite15†top L85: 
L86:            Since Linux 2.0, flock() is implemented as a system call in its
L87:            own right rather than being emulated in the GNU C library as a
L88:            call to cite22†fcntl(2) .  With this implementation, there is no
L89:            interaction between the types of lock placed by flock() and
L90:            cite22†fcntl(2) , and flock() does not detect deadlock.  (Note, however,
L91:            that on some systems, such as the modern BSDs, flock() and
L92:            cite22†fcntl(2) locks do interact with one another.)
L93: 
L94:        CIFS details
L95:            Up to Linux 5.4, flock() is not propagated over SMB.  A file with
L96:            such locks will not appear locked for remote clients.
L97: 
L98:            Since Linux 5.5, flock() locks are emulated with SMB byte-range

L107:            Remote and mandatory locking semantics may vary with SMB protocol,
L108:            mount options and server type.  See cite23†mount.cifs(8) for additional
L109:            information.

L113: ## HISTORY         cite15†top L114: 
L115:            4.4BSD (the flock() call first appeared in 4.2BSD).  A version of
L116:            flock(), possibly implemented in terms of cite22†fcntl(2) , appears on
L117:            most UNIX systems.
L118: 
L119:        NFS details
L120:            Up to Linux 2.6.11, flock() does not lock files over NFS (i.e.,
L121:            the scope of locks was limited to the local system).  Instead, one
L122:            could use cite22†fcntl(2) byte-range locking, which does work over NFS,
L123:            given a sufficiently recent version of Linux and a server which
L124:            supports locking.
L125: 
L126:            Since Linux 2.6.12, NFS clients support flock() locks by emulating
L127:            them as cite22†fcntl(2) byte-range locks on the entire file.  This means
L128:            that cite22†fcntl(2) and flock() locks do interact with one another over
L129:            NFS.  It also means that in order to place an exclusive lock, the
L130:            file must be opened for writing.
L131:            Since Linux 2.6.37, the kernel supports a compatibility mode that
L132:            allows flock() locks (and also cite22†fcntl(2) byte region locks) to be
L133:            treated as local; see the discussion of the local_lock option in
L134:            cite24†nfs(5) .
L135: ## NOTES         cite15†top L136: 
L137:            flock() places advisory locks only; given suitable permissions on
L138:            a file, a process is free to ignore the use of flock() and perform
L139:            I/O on the file.
L140: 
L141:            flock() and cite22†fcntl(2) locks have different semantics with respect
L142:            to forked processes and cite18†dup(2) .  On systems that implement flock()
L143:            using cite22†fcntl(2) , the semantics of flock() will be different from
L144:            those described in this manual page.
L145: 
L146:            Converting a lock (shared to exclusive, or vice versa) is not
L147:            guaranteed to be atomic: the existing lock is first removed, and
L148:            then a new lock is established.  Between these two steps, a
L149:            pending lock request by another process may be granted, with the
L150:            result that the conversion either blocks, or fails if LOCK_NB was
L151:            specified.  (This is the original BSD behavior, and occurs on many
L152:            other implementations.)
L153:            Release of a lock when a file descriptor is closed is not
L154:            sequenced after all observable effects of cite25†close(2) .  For example,
L155:            if one process writes a file while holding an exclusive lock, then
L156:            closes that file, and another process blocks placing a shared lock
L157:            on that file to wait until it is closed, it may observe that a
L158:            subsequent cite19†execve(2) of that file fails with ETXTBSY, and
L159:            cite26†umount(2) of its underlying filesystem fails with EBUSY, as if the
L160:            file were still open in the first process.
